newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian communists do well in local polls.
newsitem.headline: Russian communists do well in local polls.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's camp lost to the communists in a string of elections for governors in 10 Russian regions on Sunday but was narrowly ahead overall, early voting returns showed on Monday.

Candidates from the communist-led Union of National and Patriotic Forces won the governors' seats in four regions and went through as favourites to a second round in another two, Russian news agencies quoted electoral commissions as saying.
Candidates openly backed by Yeltsin's administration won in two regions and are likely winners in another two run-off votes to take place later this year.

Elections are being held for governors in 52 of Russia's 89 regions over several months up to the end of the year. Regional governors form half of the Federation Council upper house where the other half is occupied by heads of regional councils.

The communist-led opposition, which already holds a majority in the State Duma lower house of parliament, says the votes held in 40 regions so far have put them well on the path towards winning control over the Federation Council as well.
But the Kremlin says that 21 of all new governors support the government and that most of the rest are not hardline opponents.
Until now most regional governors were appointed and sacked directly by Yeltsin.

On many occasions the governors acted on Yeltsin's behalf in conflicts with largely pro-communist regional councils and as Moscow's emissaries in pushing though unpopular government decisions in their domains.
The polls mark a great change. Governors will now depend more on their voters than on the Kremlin and are likely to turn into regional lobbyists in Moscow.

In a country where wage delays have grown into a national problem and where lack of tax revenues prevents the cabinet from carrying out its financial obligations to the regions envisaged by the budget, this change may cause problems for the Kremlin.

The first sign of fresh headaches came last week, when angry members of the Federation Council blasted Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin for failing to turn up on their request. Some of them even spoke of initiating a no-confidence vote in the government.
